SUSSEX, Virginia (CNN) -- Suspended NFL quarterback Michael Vick must adhere to tightened restrictions after he tested positive for marijuana use, a federal judge said Wednesday. Suspended Atlanta Falcons quarterback Michael Vick tested positive for marijuana in a September 13 drug test. Vick tested positive for the drug on September 13, a court document from the Eastern District of Virginia shows. As a result, U.S. District Judge Henry E. Hudson ordered Vick to "submit to any method of testing required by the pretrial services officer or the supervising officer for determining whether the defendant is using a prohibited substance." Those methods could include random drug testing, a remote alcohol testing system "and/or any form of prohibited substance screening or testing," the order said. Vick, 27, must participate in substance abuse therapy and mental health counseling "if deemed advisable by the pretrial services officer or supervising officer" at his own expense, the order said. Vick was also ordered to stay home between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., "or as directed by the pretrial services officer or supervising officer," the order said. He is to be electronically monitored during that time. The conditions are to apply until Vick's sentencing, which is set for December 10.  Read about the federal case against Vick » . "This is a very difficult time for Mr. Vick," said Billy Martin, Vick's lead defense counsel, in a written statement. "He will comply with the court's new conditions regarding release." Vick faces a possible prison term of 12 to 18 months after his August guilty plea to federal conspiracy charges related to dogfighting on his property in Surry County, Virginia. The original terms of the pretrial release, set in July by U.S. Magistrate Dennis W. Dohnal, required that Vick not use narcotic drugs or other controlled substances unless prescribed by a doctor. Vick's guilty plea in the federal case came after three associates -- Purnell Peace, 35, of Virginia Beach, Virginia; Quanis Phillips, 28, of Atlanta, Georgia; and Tony Taylor, 34, of Hampton, Virginia -- admitted their roles in the operation and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors. On Tuesday, a Virginia grand jury indicted Vick and the three co-defendants on state charges of running a dogfighting ring at the home.  See a timeline of the case against Vick » . The Surry County grand jury brought two charges against Vick: one count of unlawfully torturing and killing dogs and one of promoting dogfights. Each is a felony charge that could result in a five-year prison term. Vick will be arraigned October 3 in state court in Virginia. Vick's attorneys say they are fighting the state charges on the grounds that he can't be convicted twice of the same crime. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Eric Fiegel contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
**SUSSEX, Virginia (CNN) —** Suspended NFL quarterback Michael Vick must comply with stricter restrictions after testing positive for marijuana, a federal judge said Wednesday.

The suspended Atlanta Falcons quarterback, 27, tested positive for the drug on September 13, according to a court document from the Eastern District of Virginia.

As a result, U.S. District Judge Henry E. Hudson ordered Vick to “submit to any method of testing required by the pretrial services officer or the supervising officer for determining whether the defendant is using a prohibited substance.”

Such methods could include random drug testing, a remote alcohol-testing system “and/or any form of prohibited substance screening or testing,” the order said.

Vick must also participate, at his own expense, in substance-abuse therapy and mental-health counseling “if deemed advisable by the pretrial services officer or supervising officer.”

In addition, Vick was ordered to remain at home between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m., “or as directed by the pretrial services officer or supervising officer,” and will be electronically monitored during those hours.

The conditions will remain in effect until Vick’s sentencing, which is scheduled for December 10. *Read about the federal case against Vick »*

“This is a very difficult time for Mr. Vick,” Billy Martin, Vick’s lead defense counsel, said in a written statement. “He will comply with the court’s new conditions regarding release.”

Vick faces a possible prison sentence of 12 to 18 months following his August guilty plea to federal conspiracy charges related to dogfighting on his property in Surry County, Virginia.

The original terms of his pretrial release, imposed in July by U.S. Magistrate Dennis W. Dohnal, prohibited Vick from using narcotic drugs or other controlled substances unless prescribed by a doctor.

Vick entered his guilty plea in the federal case after three associates—Purnell Peace, 35, of Virginia Beach, Virginia; Quanis Phillips, 28, of Atlanta, Georgia; and Tony Taylor, 34, of Hampton, Virginia—admitted their roles in the operation and agreed to cooperate with prosecutors.

On Tuesday, a Virginia grand jury indicted Vick and the three co-defendants on state charges related to operating a dogfighting ring at the home. *See a timeline of the case against Vick »*

The Surry County grand jury brought two charges against Vick: one count of unlawfully torturing and killing dogs and one count of promoting dogfights. Each is a felony punishable by up to five years in prison.

Vick is scheduled to be arraigned October 3 in Virginia state court. His attorneys say they are challenging the state charges on the grounds that he cannot be convicted twice of the same crime.

*E-mail to a friend.*

CNN’s Eric Fiegel contributed to this report.
outputs.L2:
**SUSSEX, Virginia (CNN)** — A federal judge imposed stricter release conditions on suspended NFL quarterback Michael Vick on Wednesday after a drug screening detected marijuana.

Court records from the Eastern District of Virginia show that the suspended Atlanta Falcons quarterback tested positive on September 13. In response, U.S. District Judge Henry E. Hudson directed Vick to undergo whatever testing the pretrial services or supervising officer requires to determine whether he is using banned substances. The screening may involve unannounced drug tests, remote alcohol monitoring, or other methods of detecting prohibited substances.

The order also requires Vick, 27, to pay for substance-abuse treatment and mental-health counseling if his supervising officer considers either necessary. In addition, he must remain at home from 10 p.m. until 6 a.m.—or during other hours specified by supervising officials—and will be monitored electronically during that period.

These restrictions will remain in place until Vick is sentenced on December 10 in the federal case.

Billy Martin, Vick’s chief defense attorney, said in a written statement that Vick is going through an extremely difficult period and will follow the court’s revised release requirements.

Vick could receive a prison sentence of 12 to 18 months after pleading guilty in August to federal conspiracy charges connected to a dogfighting operation on his property in Surry County, Virginia.

The initial pretrial-release rules, established in July by U.S. Magistrate Dennis W. Dohnal, prohibited Vick from using narcotics or other controlled substances unless they had been prescribed by a physician.

Vick entered his federal guilty plea after three associates acknowledged participating in the operation and agreed to assist prosecutors. They were Purnell Peace, 35, of Virginia Beach, Virginia; Quanis Phillips, 28, of Atlanta, Georgia; and Tony Taylor, 34, of Hampton, Virginia.

On Tuesday, a Virginia grand jury also indicted Vick and those three co-defendants on state allegations that they operated a dogfighting ring at the residence.

The Surry County grand jury charged Vick with two felonies: unlawfully torturing and killing dogs, and promoting dogfighting. Each offense carries a potential sentence of five years in prison.

Vick is scheduled to be arraigned in a Virginia state court on October 3. His lawyers plan to challenge the state prosecution by arguing that he cannot be convicted twice for the same offense.

The original report included links to additional information and a timeline of the case, as well as an option to e-mail the story to a friend. CNN’s Eric Fiegel contributed to the report.

He was also placed under a nighttime curfew and required to wear an electronic monitoring device. The new conditions were imposed because the positive drug test violated the terms of his release, which prohibited the use of illegal drugs.

Vick had pleaded guilty to participating in a conspiracy involving an interstate dogfighting operation based at property he owned in Virginia. The case led to his suspension from the NFL and put his professional football career in jeopardy.

The tightened restrictions were set to remain in effect until his December 10 sentencing. By increasing supervision rather than immediately revoking his release, the court allowed Vick to remain out of custody while making clear that further violations could lead to more severe consequences, including detention.
